## Normal approximation of binomial

When np(1-p) >= 10, a normal can be well-approximated by a binomial.  Consider Binom(500, 0.96).

```{r}
# P(X <= 478) with exact binomial probability
sum(dbinom(0:478, 500, 0.96))

# P(X <= 478 with normal approximation)
pnorm(478, 500*0.96, sqrt(500*0.96*0.04))
```


## Proportion sampling distribution

Since a sample proportion is a binomial RV multiplied by a constant, the graph of the proportion sampling distribution also looks like a binomial.

Let's simulate the proportion of heads in 10 fair coin flips.

```{r}
flips <- tibble(
  prop_heads = replicate(10000,
                         mean(sample(0:1, size = 10,
                                     replace = T, prob = c(0.5, 0.5))
                              ))
)

ggplot(flips, aes(x = prop_heads)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "goldenrod2", color = "black",
                 bins = 11)
```


## Proportion Z-test

In the powerplant example, 52% of 300 births are girls.  We have a null hypothesis of $p = 0.5$, which gives a null distribution

$$\hat{p} \;\dot{\sim}\; N(0.5, \sqrt{\frac{0.5(0.5)}{300}})$$

This gives observed test statistic 0.693.

```{r}
se <- sqrt(0.5*0.5 / 300)

test_stat <- (0.52 - 0.5) / se

test_stat
```

To calculate a two-sided p-value, we need the area above 0.693 and the area below -0.693.  We can take advantage of the fact that the standard normal is symmetric around 0.

```{r}
pnorm(-test_stat) + pnorm(test_stat, lower.tail = F)

# By symmetry
2*pnorm(test_stat, lower.tail = F)
```

EX 10.2

A survey of 15 high-school students showed that 11 of them use social media. Consider using this data to test hypotheses

$$H_0: p = 0.8 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_A: p \neq 0.8$$

with $\alpha = 0.01$.  Complete this test with both a binomial and a standard normal (Z) null distribution.

```{r}
# Binomial p-value
sum(dbinom(0:11, 15, 0.8)) +
  sum(dbinom(13:15, 15, 0.8))
```

```{r}
# Z-test (approximate)
se <- sqrt(0.8*0.2/15)

test_stat <- (11/15 - 0.8) / se

test_stat
```

```{r}
# Two-sided Z p-value
2*pnorm(test_stat)
```


Can we trust the result of the Z test?  How big does $n$ need to be before the normal approximation is appropriate?

```{r}
desired_n <- 10 / (0.8*0.2)

desired_n
```



## Proportion Z CI

To create a 99% Z confidence interval, use the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles of the standard normal.  They are positive and negative versions of the same number, since the standard normal curve is symmetric.

```{r}
qnorm(0.005)
qnorm(0.995)
```

```{r}
cv <- qnorm(0.995)

se <- sqrt(0.52*0.48 / 300)

phat <- 0.52

# 99% interval for p
c(phat - cv*se, phat + cv*se)
```


EX 10.3

Re-create the CI for the powerplant example, but use a 95% confidence level.

```{r}
# Critical values for 95% confidence
qnorm(0.025)
qnorm(0.975)
```

```{r}
# 95% Z confidence interval
cv <- qnorm(0.975)
se <- sqrt(0.52 * 0.48 / 300)
phat <- 0.52

c(phat - cv*se, phat + cv*se)
```

```{r}
# SE for proportion CI
sqrt(0.52 * 0.48 / 300)

# SE for proportion test with H0: p = 0.5
sqrt(0.5 * 0.5 / 300)
```
